subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN RADIATION MEASUREMENT PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGES IN RADIATION MEASUREMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been some changes made in my department's radiation measurement program which I feel would be of interest to the house.
As hon. members will recall, last May we set up a fluid milk sampling program at three stations which is designed to measure levels of iodine 131, a short-lived component of fall-out. By July of this year the network measuring iodine 131 was increased to seven stations, with samples being taken three times a week. Several days ago two more stations were opened, so that the network now covers Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Sault Ste. Marie, London, Ottawa, Quebec city and Halifax.
A further change has to do with the publication of results from various sectors of the measurement program. Until now these have been reported on a quarterly basis. However, developments have now reached the point where it is practical to publish findings on a monthly basis. The first of these reports should be released today. For the information of the house I might say that this report will show an increase in iodine 131 levels during the month of September. However, the accumulated levels are still substantially below those at which remedial action is considered essential to public health.
These new procedures of more frequent reporting which I mentioned earlier will, I hope, contribute to keeping the Canadian public informed on developments of the field of radiation.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MODIFICATION OF IMPORT SURCHARGES

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MODIFICATION OF IMPORT SURCHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement concerning the import surcharges which were instituted in June to deal with the critical exchange situation. These measures have been kept under constant review by the government, and in the
light of representations which have now been received from Canadian businessmen and individuals, firms and corporations, certain adjustments have been made to remove anomalies and to deal with hardship cases.
1 am now glad to be able to inform the house that in the light of our improved foreign exchange position a first major step is being taken toward the removal of these surcharges. Effective immediately the surcharges are being removed from industrial machinery and equipment not made in Canada, wherever such equipment is separately classified in the tariff.
The surcharges are also being removed from two products which must be imported for use in Canadian manufacturing. One is wide steel sheets for use in the manufacture of bathtub stampings. The other is corn used in making starch and a number of other products also used in the House of Commons. The surcharge was removed from corn for agricultural purposes some time ago, and all corn will now be free of surcharge regardless of use.
The removal of these surcharges will assist Canadian industry in becoming more competitive here in Canada and in export markets. It also meets some of the legitimate concerns of our trading partners whose trade interests have been affected. The Prime Minister has made clear that the surcharges are temporary in nature and will be removed as soon as our circumstances permit. I am sure that this house and the trading community, both in Canada and abroad, will welcome this present move.

speechtext: Has the Prime Minister issued any public statement on (a) the propriety of ministers holding directorships or executive positions with private corporations or (b) the propriety of ministers holding shares of private corporations and, if so, when was the statement made and what was the gist of it on each of these matters?

subtopic: DIRECTORSHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in regard to part (a) there has been no issue of a statement as such, although there have been references made by me from time to time in the house and elsewhere. The effect of these utterances is that members of the cabinet should upon their appointment resign any directorships held in business corporations. On June 20, 1961, as found at page 6599 of Hansard, I emphasized that the policy of the present government when it came into power was to ensure that no minister in the cabinet would hold a portfolio while at the same time having a position as director of any company.

However plans for the further extension and improvement of modern electronic and other aids to navigation covering the approaches to Halifax over the coming years may, in due course, require consideration of the lightship, which does not itself mark any hazard. It may be it will be found that in due course its purpose can be more effectively carried out by modern means which provide precise positioning over a much wider segment of the approach area, but this remains to be seen.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO STRENGTH OF ARMED FORCES ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in that connection I think perhaps I had better point out to the hon. member and to the house that the numbers in the armed forces at the present time are very considerably increased over what they were a year ago. maintopic: ESQUIMALT, B.C.-REGULATIONS RESPECTING POLITICAL ACTIVITIES OF CIVILIAN EMPLOYEES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: ESQUIMALT, B.C.-REGULATIONS RESPECTING POLITICAL ACTIVITIES OF CIVILIAN EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
On Monday last, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands asked a question relating to a notice having been posted at the dockyard at Esquimau. This was alleged to have been a section of the civilian personnel administrative and accounting manual, and according to the hon. member the substance of the notice was to the effect that any civilian employee was prohibited from contributing to any funds of any political party on or off the premises, or taking part in any partisan activity on or off the premises. I said at that time that I would look into the matter.
I have now been informed that the notice in question was a direct quotation from section 61 of the Civil Service Act. The relevant part of section 61 reads as follows:

No deputy head or employee shall contribute, receive, or in any way deal with any money for the funds of any political party.
As the house is aware, the Civil Service Act was passed in the house unanimously on September 20, 1961.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED REALLOCATION OF FINANCIAL BURDEN
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED REALLOCATION OF FINANCIAL BURDEN
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the federal government should give leadership by convening a conference of federal, provincial and municipal authorities to review the responsibilities of each level of government and their financial ability to assume same, with a view to reallocating the heavy burden for services, such as education and welfare on a more equitable basis.

Equitable Division of Tax Burden
He said: Mr. Speaker, no question is dealt with more often in the newspapers from one end of Canada to the other than the plight of the local taxpayers and their feeling that the cost of municipal government is now exorbitant. Old age pensioners living on a fixed income complain that the increases each year are forcing them to move from homes in which they have lived for generations. Young people establishing themselves for the first time are finding it increasingly difficult to meet local taxes which can range from $250 to $400 a year for quite modest homes. Tremendous increases in local taxes are not the result of extravagance or mismanagement by local municipalities. Nor can it be argued that municipalities are rushing into new fields unthinkingly. On the contrary, local municipalities are moving too slowly in meeting their responsibilities, and they themselves know it; but they are completely hamstrung by their present needs and responsibilities.
Local taxes have doubled and tripled because of the tremendous urban growth and expansion since world war II. Municipal services, utilities such as water, sewers and power, have been expanded, as have educational plant and other community facilities. Until this century it was thought that municipal governments which possessed their own sources of taxation and other revenues were able to provide for their own needs and to finance them. But since world war II it has become obvious that services such as education, public welfare, unemployment relief and health be financed by municipal governments. Therefore we have seen increasing financial participation by provincial and federal governments in these services and in other municipal undertakings in fields such as slum clearance and low rental housing. Without such assistance the municipalities would not have been able to maintain their normal services and to begin to catch up on some-and only a little-of the backlog of needed public works which were deferred during the depression of the thirties and during world war II. But even with this aid, Mr. Speaker, municipal debt has grown from $1 billion in 1950 to over $4 billion in 1960. This debt has become a first charge on municipal revenues, and will be so for generations to come.
This tremendous change has taken place in urban Canada because municipal governments are forced to assume responsibilities never contemplated when the basic municipal tax structure was established, and this change is still going on. In 1900 the tax on property could take care of most municipal


needs. The explosion in Canadian population since then and the movement of more and more people to the cities each year has meant the establishment of new and ever more costly services. These are in fact more provincial and federal in character than they are municipal. The costs are still being borne, to a great extent, by the municipal governments, but they have pushed the municipal governments to the limit.
The financial problems of local urban governments cannot be solved within the present bounds of existing municipal tax revenue structure. Municipal taxes have gone up from $483 million in 1950 to $1,349 million in 1960, an increase of almost 300 per cent. Mr. Speaker, this is not surprising at all if we examine how the municipal bill for education alone has gone up. I want to make it very clear that I for one do not think we are spending too much money on education. If anything, we are spending much too little. In fact, there are few, if any, countries in the western world who are spending as little on education as are we in Canada. If you compare five cities in five different provinces in the last ten years, you see a very interesting and real problem. In the city of Vancouver in 1951 the local municipality paid $7 million for education; in 1961 the cost had risen to $16.5 million. In the city of Winnipeg in 1951 the local government paid $5.8 million for education; in 1961 $14.1 million. In Edmonton the cost of education has gone from $4.8 million in 1951 to $15.1 million in 1961. In Toronto the cost has gone from $18.8 million in 1951 to $45.8 million in 1961. And in Montreal it has gone from $17 million in 1951 to $38.6 million in 1961. In brief, Mr. Speaker, school costs alone in these five large cities in five different provinces have more than doubled, and in some cases have tripled, in just ten years, and the prospects for the next ten years are just as dismal and just as dangerous for the municipalities. Is it any wonder that local taxpayers are up in arms?
Education costs are just one example of what has happened at the local government level. Urban renewal, express highways, hospitals, bridges, are just a few of the things needed with which the local governments are having to cope. Municipal governments are not looking for handouts. They know their responsibilities; but they do say that this kind of local need can be met only through genuine partnerships between the federal, the provincial and the municipal governments. Tremendous social capital is required if they are to begin to meet the needs of the near future. Municipal governments feel that the aid of the federal government is required as never before.

Equitable Division of Tax Burden
The municipalities know that they were created by the provinces. But they believe that the federal and provincial governments have a vital stake in their financial wellbeing. They believe that urban growth and the changing needs of the urban population have given to municipal governments problems or responsibilities which they can no longer discharge without a fundamental increase in aid from the senior governments. The municipalities appreciate the increased aid they have received in recent years from both the provincial and the federal governments, but they believe that the aid so far given has been too little, too late, and too uncertain. They believe it is necessary now to reassess and re-evaluate the duties and responsibilities of all governments and their financial resources.
At its 1961 conference, the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities passed a resolution which I should like to read into the record. It is as follows:
Be it resolved that once again the government of Canada be petitioned to initiate a meeting at which representatives of the three levels of government can confer for the purpose of re-evaluating their respective fields of administrative responsibility and to discuss ways and means to re-allocate the sources of revenue available to them in the field of taxation.
Mr. Speaker, my resolution urges the house and the government to follow the sensible suggestion proposed by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. This proposal has been seriously and thoughtfully presented by the federation. It has the support of the vast majority of the local municipal councils across Canada. It is a matter of urgent and vital concern to every local taxpayer who has been called upon to pay substantially higher local taxes almost every year. Such a conference would help bring order and justice into the relationship between the three levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal, and it deserves the support of every hon. member of this house.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED REALLOCATION OF FINANCIAL BURDEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North on bringing forward this resolution for the consideration of the house. It calls for the federal government to take the leadership in convening a conference such as he has outlined of federal, provincial and municipal authorities to review the responsibilities of each level of government, and their financial ability to assume those responsibilities. Then we come to the meat of the resolution, namely the subject of financing education and social welfare. We might begin with a brief review of the responsibilities of the various levels of government. Under the British North America
Act education is dealt with in a completely separate section, namely section 93. It is set forth as follows:
93. In and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and according to the following provisions:-
There are then outlined four subsections which aim to take care of the minorities in the various provinces. In section 91 of the act the legislative powers of the federal government are outlined. In it there is nothing about education or social welfare. In section 92 the powers of the provincial legislatures are outlined, and in subsection 7 we find the following:
7. The establishment, maintenance, and management of hospitals, asylums, charities, and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other than marine hospitals.
Subsection 8 reads as follows:
8 Municipal institutions in the province.
This resolution proposes a conference between the federal, provincial and municipal authorities. There is some question as to the propriety of mentioning municipalities in this respect. As pointed out in subsection 8 of section 92 of the British North America Act, the sole responsibility for municipal institutions is left with the provincial government. Therefore if any conference is held it should be a conference between the federal government and the provinces. We might point out that very many of such conferences have been held to deal with these problems. The establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals and so on is also a provincial responsibility.
Years ago, at the time of confederation and for some time following, the responsibilities of the various levels of government in Canada were clearly defined. They were quite distinct. Methods of travel then were much slower than they are today. The means of communication was not so efficient as they are today. Local government at the municipal level had their own problems quite separate and distinct from the provincial problems and federal problems. The local problems consisted of the provision of roads, bridges, schools and other matters of purely local concern. Their materials and their labour were all local and much of the work was paid for through labour. It is not so many years ago that, in the province of Ontario, statutory labour went out of practice as far as the maintenance of our roads is concerned. I can well remember when every farmer in the rural areas was compelled by law to put in so many hours work or so many days work on the roads of his municipality. It was called statute labour. In the wintertime he was conpelled by law, if called upon to do

Equitable Division of Tax Burden so, to get out and clear the roads of snow. He was subject to penalties if he did not answer the call of the official who was then known as the pathmaster whose responsibility it was to keep the roads clear of snow.
The point I am trying to make is that in those days municipal government and municipal matters were quite separate and distinct from the higher levels of government. As time went on and standards were raised, roads became more expensive, power machinery was introduced and the old methods had to be discarded. No longer do we find the farmers working out their taxes on the roads. There is now in use for municipal purposes extremely heavy machinery which is much more efficient in clearing the roads of snow and in building roads. However, the old insulation is gone. Municipal affairs became more and more of interest to the province. The small municipalities were unable on their own to purchase the heavy equipment which was required and to build the more expensive types of roads. A system of grants therefore developed and the province began to subsidize the municipalities. It helped out the weaker municipalities and it served as a sharing of the wealth between the wealthier sections and the poorer sections of the province.
The same trend applies to education. In the early days the local people built their own schools of logs or other local materials. As time went on, standards were raised and the schools became more expensive. The cost of maintaining those schools became greater. More schools were required. More education was required. This trend has gone on until, of recent years, the little old red school-house has practically disappeared from the landscape and we have fine new central schools all across the country, at least in many areas. The costs have gone up. Again, in order to transfer some of the wealth from the larger urban centres to the small and weaker communities scattered across the country, the system of grants was developed. I think this system of grants is working very well indeed. However, the control is left in the hands of the local people. While the grants from the senior levels of government help to meet the expenses, the control is left with the local people. The control is left with the local people also in matters of welfare; and we have today our joint programs of welfare, with the cost shared largely by the federal and provincial governments and with the municipalities taking only that share of the cost which is sufficient to keep them interested in an economical administration of these programs.
It is true that the local people are carrying a great burden of taxation, but their situation
[Mr. Thomas.1

is not too desperate. For instance, we do not want to do anything, I believe, to interfere with local control. There is a special program of taxation being applied in the province of British Columbia whereby the small homeowner is exempted from most of the taxes on his home. We also have the right of the cities and urban areas in Ontario to apply special rates of assessment against the homeowner. For this reason I believe it would be unwise to take any action or adopt any policy which would tend to centralize greater control in the senior government and remove control in some measure from the municipalities.
I think that this government does feel that the rights and interests of the local governments should be protected as far as possible and I could not support any suggestion to centralize more authority in the senior government at the expense of the local governments. Our present program is working well and it is serving to spread the wealth from the areas where it appears in the greatest concentration to those areas which need assistance. While it is not stated in the resolution, I am opposed to any implication or suggestion that our present method of financing education and social welfare is inefficient or unfair because I believe the system is working very well. Within the present framework which we have set up in this country I think we can proceed to provide the services that are required by the people without destroying the local control which in my opinion is so essential to the well-being of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker, the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas), said that he thinks the system of taxation and control is working very well. I would point out to him that, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) said, the resolution introduced by that hon. member is very much along the lines of one presented to the government by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities. This body is made up of municipal representatives from all parts of Canada and of all political parties, and I would emphasize the point that they are far from satisfied.
I am not sure that members of the house who have not had experience in municipal government in recent years realize the enormity of the problems faced by local council. I refer particularly to councils in large urban areas where they have very heavy demands made upon them. I have just completed four years on the council of a very large urban area and I realize, as a few other hon. members probably do, the problems that come up week by week and the very heavy demands made upon the local budget and consequently

upon the local taxpayer. These are very real problems and, as I say, I do not think that members of this house who have not had the experience of struggling with them in recent years can quite appreciate them.
This problem will continue to grow and I suggest that in a very few years we are going to have something of an urban revolt on our hands in Canada. I think the people of the urban centres are being shortchanged in several ways. We have had some discussion recently concerning representation in this house and in most of the provincial legislatures, and I believe that the people in the larger centres are certainly shortchanged in that respect. They also appear to be with respect to the distribution of taxation revenues both from the federal government and from their individual provincial governments. They are at the grumbling stage now, but in a very few years I think they will take a much greater interest in the subject.
Not many provincial and federal elections have been fought on the basis of what to do about municipal and civic problems, but I think that day is coming and in my opinion all political parties in Canada should look at this problem and come up with programs that will help to solve the problem faced in cities. I do not think there is any party in Canada at the present time, including my own, that has a good platform on the question of municipal and civic problems.
This is a very important matter and the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North simply seeks to have the problem tackled. We are not suggesting what all the solutions would be, but simply that the problem should be recognized and its solution undertaken. The hon. member for Middlesex West raised some objection to any financing of education from federal sources. I think there is ample precedent for this. In fact, it is being done now. Just this morning I received a letter from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) informing me that a secondary school in my municipality of Burnaby had received a grant for the building of new shops. I think there is ample precedent both at the secondary school level and the university level for federal aid in this connection. However, that is only part of the larger problem of the re-allocation of financial sources so far as the three levels of government are concerned.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is one point that we have to deal with here. I know that the question always comes up as to who will pay for this? It is pointed out that all governments have very great demands made upon them and how can they have the funds to meet these demands. I should like to conclude by reminding hon. members that the federal

Equitable Division of Tax Burden government is spending money in certain ways which I think could be spent more usefully elsewhere. We are spending a good deal of money on what we call defence. I suppose this is defence against the communist world, but I would suggest that if some of that money were re-allocated for education this would be a much better form of defence for us. I would hope that this resolution or one along these lines would receive passage this year because we cannot put off forever the problem of solving the financial difficulties of the cities and municipalities of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat that the motion now before us calls our attention to a very serious matter; and I tend to disagree with what the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) said. As we all know, in this country we have one of the most complicated forms of government. It is a form of government in which there are at least three echelons, and in the nature of things it is very doubtful that we will ever attain a perfect distribution of responsibilities and financial resources. Things are always going to be more or less unsatisfactory, I submit. But here I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) that we should not relax and drift along. Rather, we should remain alert and try to readjust ourselves to new situations and new circumstances as they develop.
We are, I think, living under a new situation and new circumstances. It is true that our constitutional arrangement is an old one. It is true also, Mr. Speaker, that by practice and by legal alteration we have modified that constitutional structure somewhat to suit our new circumstances. What we find is that our economy and our society are becoming more and more tightly integrated so that developments on the national scene now impinge upon activities which were once thought to be local and private, of concern to the individual or family, school district, or municipality. In order to get a job or to survive in our society, the individual must have certain kinds of education and certain kinds of services. For the individual, there is in this society no escape. The relationship is reciprocal. If the individual is to make a contribution to our nation he must have those same kinds of education, those same kinds of services.
We must undertake, therefore, not simply by reading certain sections of the British North America Act, 1867, to assure in the interests of both the individual and the nation that these kinds of education and these kinds of services are generally available. Let me refer for a minute to precollege education. Many of the
644	HOUSE OF
Equitable Division of Tax Burden young men and young women of Nova Scotia, for example, leave that province-reluctantly, of course-to find jobs or positions in other parts of Canada. I hear a seconding response from across the floor, and I realize that I have finally spoken the truth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED REALLOCATION OF FINANCIAL BURDEN
speechtext: They are spreading civilization.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED REALLOCATION OF FINANCIAL BURDEN
speechtext:
These young men and these young women are taking their developed talents, their time and energy, and giving them to other societies across the country. We are, of course, sorry to see them go but we realize this movement is part of the natural order of things. For the moment, Mr. Speaker, the burden of conferring this education upon those young people-I am using Nova Scotia as an example-is falling upon the people of the province. This burden is especially heavy in the case of a province such as Nova Scotia where it has to be a tax burden on what is generally unproductive property, that is houses and facilities for living which are not part of the productive portion of our economy.
This high cost of education, which in the national interest is absolutely indispensable, is taxing some of our Nova Scotia municipalities to desperation. Here I am not speaking merely in terms of generality, because I know of specific instances where this is true, specific instances where the tax rate is so high I am sure the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) would be quite horrified and would not stay there. Education, which used to be a matter of local concern, has become a matter of national concern. Yet, the primary financial responsibility for education rests with the locality. Something of the same anachronism, something of the same inability to adjust to the new times, is found in some of the welfare fields. I feel that this is a situation which is going to grow worse.
For example, sir, the winter works program may be beneficial to towns and cities where certain kinds of projects need to be done and where there is a certain amount of financial competence to enter upon these projects. However, the program fails to hit the bull's eye in the target in many of our poorer municipalities. As I say, the situation may grow worse. We have heard something from the official opposition and the other opposition party of the need for social capital investment in our affluent society. Now, if this investment is to be a municipal investment aided by partial grants or by long term loans, I suspect that quite a number of our municipalities will be left hopelessly behind because they simply will not be able


to participate. I submit that to both the official opposition and to the other opposition party.
Now, it may be argued, Mr. Speaker, that a province such as Nova Scotia intervenes to help its municipalities to meet their responsibilities. Indeed, this argument has been made. This is true, but the financial ability of a province such as Nova Scotia-I am sure that there are other provinces similarly situated-is severely limited.
This brings us to the iniquitous principle underlying the new federal-provincial tax sharing agreements. The fact that the hon. member for Middlesex West is from one of the most prosperous provinces in this country probably explains why he did not refer to this iniquitous principle. In the very short run this principle is of some advantage to Nova Scotia. However, in the not so very long run, this principle will be highly disadvantageous. The Atlantic provinces adjustment grants are fixed. The equalization payments under the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements will be based on the annual average yield of the three standard taxes rather than the yield in the two highest provinces, as formerly. The great argument in defence of the new arrangement is that it gives the provinces the right to impose their own personal income taxes. This argument, I think, appeals to the hon. member for Middlesex West, but it is not an argument that appeals to me. It is an argument that is relevant only to those provinces in which there is a comparatively high level of personal income. If this new principle is followed for long, provinces such as Nova Scotia will be less and less able to assist the municipalities.
I think it would be a tragedy, Mr. Speaker, if our municipalities and some of our provinces were unable to finance these services which are essential to our nation, essential educational programs, essential welfare programs. It would be national folly if the municipalities and some of our provinces were not able to provide these services, while millions of dollars are spent on defence establishments which are certainly of very dubious value. So, Mr. Speaker, I concur with the hon. member for Winnipeg North that the motion which he has set forth calls to our attention a matter of first rate importance, a matter which requires urgent action.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTED REALLOCATION OF FINANCIAL BURDEN
speechtext:
Before I comment on the remarks made by other hon. gentlemen in this house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to convey to you my sincere congratulations on your elevation to this high office. The main problem facing Canadian municipalities and, consequently, Canadian

taxpayers today, is not necessarily the cost of services rendered by local governments, but rather the allocation of those costs. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North pointed out, there is an ever increasing burden of taxation being imposed on all property owners for the costs of education and welfare services. Indeed the cost of education alone is perhaps the largest single factor Canadian taxpayers have to face today. It is an item which will continue to grow, and if the present trend continues, especially in our urban municipalities, we shall see each year in Canada a new city, or the equivalent of a new city with population of some 80,000 citizens.
In my humble opinion increased grants from federal or provincial authorities are not in themselves the answer. They are merely a deferment of the basic problem itself. The existence of our Canadian provinces and municipalities goes back to the Baldwin Act of 1849 and the British North America Act. These statutes set out the constitutional responsibilities and have clearly defined the precept that municipalities are creatures of the provinces. Consequently throughout succeeding years the federal government has made grants and contributions and entered into tax sharing agreements with the municipalities through their parent provinces. As the size of municipalities grows-and in some cases they are now larger than our smaller provinces-and as their administration becomes more complex, they seek ways and means of streamlining and modernizing their functions to meet the current needs of a vibrant population.
There are many municipal associations across our country and the subject of tax sharing responsibilities comes up at each of their annual conventions and regional meetings. The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities is notable among these in its search for good dominion-provincial relations, and the representations which have been made have resulted in a substantial difference in the payments to municipalities through their parent provinces.
Recent studies have been made on the composition and financing of local government, and I am happy to inform hon. members that the latest and perhaps most notable of these concluded just last month with the return to Canada of a number of Ontario elected and appointed officials representing Ontario municipalities and the provincial government, who spent several weeks in the United Kingdom, western Europe and the Scandinavian countries where they studied the structure and taxation methods adopted in those countries.
Equitable Division of Tax Burden
The association of Ontario counties, to the directorate of which the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Stenson) and myself have the honour to belong, has for the past three years been undertaking a detailed study of the various types of municipal government administration and their financial and other relationships with the province. It has also been undertaking a very significant study of similar forms of government in the states of New York, Michigan and Florida. Mr. Delby J. Bucknall, president of this association, is one of the group I mentioned earlier, as well as Mr. Allan F. Stewart, clerk-treasurer of Wentworth county and a number of other notable men in public life in the province of Ontario.
The Ontario provincial legislature has recently appointed a special committee to inquire into and make recommendations on the Ontario municipal act and other related acts, with a view to suggesting amending legislation which would recognize and meet the changing conditions in the province, and most pronounced, the change which has taken place in our society brought about by instant communication and rapid transportation.
Over the years the federal government has entered into a number of programs which are of interest to municipalities, and have directly offset the sharp upswing in municipal taxes paid by property owners. Federal-municipal programs, tax sharing agreements, and grants in lieu of taxes are not new terms in this house and I believe all hon. members, being aware of the problems in their constituent municipalities, will agree with me that these burdens have been somewhat lessened by legislation and action on these matters undertaken by this government and, indeed, by legislation which was introduced by the government of hon. members opposite.
Being cognizant of our responsibilities to the taxpayers, as we all must be, our first consideration has to be the redistribution of this so-called wealth along more equitable lines. To this end I suggest that the findings of the royal commission on taxation, which has already commenced its proceedings, will make available to this house the necessary information to formulate a policy which the hon. member for Winnipeg North seeks in his resolution. I would also respectfully point out to the hon. member that studies are currently underway in several other provinces to suggest the re-allocation of financing which he desires.
The challenge which lies before our municipal leaders in moulding the future of Canada's local government is perhaps best illustrated by the words of the Hon. Fred M. Cass, Q.C., minister of municipal affairs for Ontario, speaking to the delegates attending

Equitable Division of Tax Burden the twenty fifth annual conference of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities in Winnipeg last June. He said:
If we are to achieve the basic goal of providing a better community life for our people, we must have an intelligently informed people-a public aware of the problems and costs, and a public willing to accept the responsibilities and obligations of our way of life.
The Baldwin Act, commonly referred to as the confederation act of local government in Canada, which established our provincial-municipal relationships, has been amended from time to time as the need for change has arisen; but perhaps one of the most recent and significant changes to take place in this field was the action by the Alberta legislature in the development of their county system of government, in which a greater control by elected officials was given in matters of education financing and administration.
This trend towards localization, yet centralization of tax collecting and tax spending, is viewed with alarm in some quarters. Among some there is a fear of losing local autonomy and local identity. This may be seen where local municipal elections are won or lost on the simple issue of a central school. In addition to this we can see an endless parade of annexation and amalgamation hearings necessitated by the desire for more industrial assessment, and pointing out the obvious need for changes in our taxing laws. I have every confidence that the capable personnel of the commission currently undertaking this study will be supplied with sufficient representations from our provinces and municipal associations so as to make their findings a complete reflection of the Canadian scene.

speechtext:
My practice in other sessions was to announce the business for the following week on Thursday evening and not earlier than that. Tomorrow we shall be continuing the order of business we had hoped to reach today. The first item will be the resolution in the name of the Minister of Agriculture dealing with the Farm Credit Act, No. 24 on today's order paper. Second, we would take the second reading of Bill No. C-3 to amend the Food and Drugs Act, No. 2 on today's order paper and, after that, three items standing in the name of the Minister of Transport-second reading of Bill No. C-58 to amend the Carriage by Air Act, No. 9 on the order paper; second reading of Bill No. C-59, to approve an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Ontario, which is No. 10 on the order paper, and the resolution to amend the Aeronautics Act, which is No. 21 on the order paper.
On Friday we hope to move into supply to ask for interim supply for a period of one month, as is normal under the circumstances.

speechtext: Will we consider interim supply on Friday, even though we may not have disposed of the several items the leader of the house has announced for Thursday?

speechtext: I will leave that open to see what progress we make tomorrow. If the house deals with the five items it will be easy to go into interim supply.
